quote: Many philosophers—particularly amateur philosophers, and ancient philosophers—share a dangerous instinct: If you give them a question, they try to answer it.
content: The method the essay is about to recommend, dissolving a question by exhibiting the confusion that generates it, was the dominant program of twentieth-century philosophy. Wittgenstein wrote that “the philosophical problems should completely disappear” (Philosophical Investigations §133), Carnap’s Pseudoproblems in Philosophy (1928) applied the method to realism and the external world, Ryle diagnosed the mind–body problem as a category mistake (The Concept of Mind, 1949), and the whole of ordinary-language philosophy was a school of dissolvers. The essay presents “the philosopher’s instinct” as answering and dissolution as its own discovery; the actual professional instinct for most of the last century was the reverse, and it is the essay’s positive proposal, that dissolution must be completed by a cognitive-science account of the intuition, that has a shorter pedigree. Even that is not new: Hume’s account of why we believe in necessary connection (custom, and the mind’s propensity to spread itself on objects) is a stack trace of exactly the requested kind, written in 1739, and the essay’s Mind Projection Fallacy is Hume’s “spreading” under another name.

quote: It is a fact about human psychology that people think they have free will.
content: It is not one fact, and the experimental work on what people actually think had begun before this essay was written. When lay participants are given a described deterministic universe and asked whether an agent in it acts freely and is responsible, majorities say yes for concrete cases and no for abstract ones (Nahmias et al. (2005); Nichols & Knobe (2007)), the pattern replicates across cultures (Sarkissian et al. (2010)), and the folk concept turns out to be a bundle of framing-sensitive judgments rather than a single intuition that “free will exists.” This matters for the homework problem, because a stack trace of “the” algorithm that produces “the” free-will intuition presupposes that there is one; the data suggest there are at least two, an abstract incompatibilist one and a concrete compatibilist one, produced by different processes. The essay’s premise, that there is a stable psychological fact awaiting explanation, is the kind of premise it elsewhere tells the reader to check before dissolving anything.

quote: But when you’re really done, you’ll know you’re done. Dissolving the question is an unmistakable feeling—once you experience it, and, having experienced it, resolve not to be fooled again. Those who dream do not know they dream, but when you wake you know you are awake.
content: The criterion of completion offered here is a feeling, and the feeling has been studied: it is not a reliable signal. The “Aha!” experience accompanies false insights as readily as true ones (Danek & Wiley (2017) found that solutions reported with the full phenomenology of insight were wrong a substantial fraction of the time and that the feeling did not discriminate), feelings of knowing predict retrieval only weakly (Metcalfe (1986)), and the sense that a problem has been resolved is exactly what the essay elsewhere calls a curiosity-stopper. The dream analogy is wrong in both directions: lucid dreamers know they are dreaming (LaBerge et al. (1981) demonstrated it with pre-agreed eye signals), and false awakenings are the experience of being sure one is awake while asleep. The essay concedes that the reverse implication fails (feeling done does not mean being done), which makes the criterion useless as a check, since the only case in which one would consult it is the case in which it cannot be trusted. What remains is the essay’s worked example, the tree in the forest, dissolved by a network diagram that Book III’s annotations found untested and, where tested, wrong.

quote: For example, there can be a dangling unit in the center of a neural network, which does not correspond to any real thing, or any real property of any real thing, existent anywhere in the real world. This dangling unit is often useful as a shortcut in computation, which is why we have them. (Metaphorically speaking. Human neurobiology is surely far more complex.)
content: The parenthesis withdraws the mechanism in the same breath as offering it. Book III’s Neural Categories drew two toy networks, gave them properties (Network 1 “oscillates,” Network 2 has a central node), and used the second to explain why people argue about trees; the annotations there recorded that the properties are wrong for the networks drawn, that the psychological model Network 2 formalizes (feature-similarity categorization, naive Bayes) was tested against causal-model accounts and lost (Rehder (2003)), and that no study has ever connected the “dangling unit” to the phenomenology of a residual question. This essay then asks the reader to hold the diagram to the standard of a “full and satisfactory descriptive explanation of how each intuitive sensation arises, point by point,” and declares the tree question dissolved by it. By the standard the essay sets out, the diagram is an “explaining why” dressed as an “explaining how”: it names a component that would, if it existed, produce the feeling, and the evidence that it exists is that the feeling occurs. The essay calls this a stack trace. It is a hypothesis, and it is one that its author disclaims as metaphor in the same sentence.
